drills.q: Why does a naive PDF text extractor fail on a two-column layout, and why is the failure dangerous?
drills.a: It reads content in the PDF's internal object order, which for two columns is often interleaved line-by-line across columns, producing fluent but semantically scrambled text. It's dangerous because no exception is thrown and nothing looks obviously broken -- it can survive all the way to a confidently wrong answer.

drills.q: Compare markdown serialization, per-row records, and summary+reference for table handling. When would you pick each?
drills.a: Markdown serialization (default, small-medium tables). Per-row records when the full markdown exceeds the chunk budget -- split by row, header carried along, row index as metadata. Summary+reference for very large/wide tables where per-row chunking produces too many near-duplicate low-signal chunks.

drills.q: Why must code be split on AST boundaries instead of character or line counts, and what happens when a single function is still too large?
drills.a: Character/line splitting can cut a function mid-body or drop its enclosing class/import context, producing an unusable fragment. AST-aware splitting via tree-sitter guarantees syntactically complete chunks; for an oversized function, real implementations recurse into nested AST boundaries (blocks, statements) rather than falling back to a raw character cut.

drills.q: What is parent-child hierarchical retrieval and what specific problem does it solve that one flat chunk size can't?
drills.a: Small leaf chunks are indexed for precise similarity search, but the parent chunk is substituted at retrieval time when enough children are retrieved together (LlamaIndex AutoMergingRetriever). It solves documents whose sections vary widely in natural density -- a short definition and a dense multi-page procedure can't both be served well by one chunk size.

drills.q: Why is an image caption a lossy representation, and what's the practical consequence for retrieval?
drills.a: A caption compresses the image's full information into text, so retrieval only succeeds for queries the caption's text actually captures. A vague caption gives retrieval nothing to match a specific query against even though the answer is visible in the image -- caption quality directly bounds which queries can succeed.

drills.q: What can knowledge-graph RAG answer that flat chunk retrieval structurally cannot, and what's its real cost profile?
drills.a: Multi-hop questions connecting facts across documents and whole-corpus 'global' summary questions. Cost: ~3-5x token inflation for entity/relation extraction, early indexing runs around $33k for a large corpus, and 2-3x higher query latency from graph traversal -- though indexing cost has dropped to roughly 0.1% of that within ~18 months via better prompting/caching.

drills.q: A PDF ingestion pipeline works well on single-column test documents but silently degrades once multi-column financial statements with tables start flowing in. Diagnose.
drills.a: The test set almost certainly didn't exercise multi-column or table-heavy layouts, so the parser's reading-order and table-flattening behavior was never validated. Diagnose by comparing extracted text against the source document's visual layout on the actual failing documents -- the existing eval structurally can't surface this class of bug if it never included these document shapes.

drills.q: When is it wrong to build a parent-child hierarchy or a knowledge graph, even though both are more sophisticated than flat chunking?
drills.a: Parent-child hierarchies waste complexity on short, structurally flat documents (FAQs, tickets) with no meaningful density variation across sections. Knowledge graphs waste cost and latency on corpora/query patterns that are fundamentally single-hop lookup rather than multi-hop/relational -- profile actual query patterns before adopting either.

drills.q: Design the ingestion pipeline for a corpus mixing scanned invoices, a multi-column technical report, a codebase, and a 300-page policy manual.
drills.a: Route by detected source type before chunking: OCR fallback (triggered by text-density detection) plus per-row table serialization for invoices; a layout-aware parser validated for multi-column reading order (Docling/Marker-PDF) with tables serialized to markdown for the report; tree-sitter AST-boundary splitting for the codebase; parent-child hierarchical chunking with auto-merging for the policy manual since its sections vary widely in density. Every unit carries provenance metadata (source type, extraction method, document/page/section ID) so ingestion failures are diagnosable separately from retrieval or generation failures.

drills.q: Would you build a knowledge graph across a corpus of invoices, reports, and policies just because they're relationally connected in principle?
drills.a: Only if the actual query pattern requires multi-hop reasoning across those sources (e.g. 'which invoices reference a vendor mentioned in this policy exception'). If most real queries are single-source lookups, the graph's cost and latency tax isn't justified regardless of how relationally connected the underlying data theoretically is.
